summary: In this fiction excerpt from Book 14, the narrator arranges to stay overnight at a lake cottage in Sibley County with a school friend, deliberately planting a clue about Henry Hastings Sibley so that Monica will understand the narrator is doing something risky while being told it is safe. Nikko, whose parents are unreachable, proposes borrowing a car from Bree, a purple-haired girl who tabled for the Solidarity Committee at a protest over unfair arrests. The narrator objects that Bree would be put at risk, and Nikko's accusation that the narrator is irrational leads to a tense exchange before he backpedals.
one_line: A narrator arranges a risky overnight trip to Sibley County and Nikko proposes borrowing Bree's car, sparking tension over her safety.
key_facts: The narrator is arranging an overnight stay with a school friend whose family has a lake cottage in Sibley County.
The friend's family cottage has a wood stove and a dog described as a good watchdog.
The narrator chose Sibley County deliberately because both people thought there were too many monuments and places named after Henry Hastings Sibley.
The narrator worries that someone from the Joint Terrorism Task Force could be listening in on the phone call.
Monica says "I love you" to the narrator, and the narrator replies "Love you, too" while wondering if they had ever said it out loud before.
Nikko's father is in court today and his mother is out of town on a business trip.
Nikko proposes borrowing a car from a girl named Bree, who has purple hair.
Nikko says Bree would be willing to share the driving on what he calls a long trip.
The narrator says Bree was at the protest, where she was tabling for the Solidarity Committee.
The narrator dismisses the Solidarity Committee as people who decided to own the cause and just want to get on television.
Nikko tells the narrator that the narrator is not being very rational.
The narrator says that being told they are not rational makes them see red and that their fists were already clenched.
Nikko apologizes and backpedals after the narrator's reaction, saying he should not have said that.
